page2_img_1.png.title: Adapted knowledge-worker actions for software engineers
page2_img_1.png.description: A one-page table that defines the set of knowledge-worker actions the authors adapted for the software engineering domain (Table I). Each row names an action (e.g., Learning; Analyze; Authoring; Co-authoring; Dissemination; Expert Search; Feedback; Information Organization; Information Search; Monitoring; Networking; Service Search) and gives a short definition plus concrete examples tailored to developers — for example, Analyze includes understanding unfamiliar code and debugging; Authoring is independent code or documentation; Co-authoring is writing code with a team; Expert Search is finding someone to help fix a bug; Information Search includes locating bug reports, specs, or API docs. The paper uses these instantiated actions as the basis for the weekly hours questions in the survey and for clustering engineers into personas.

page7_img_table_1.png.title: Collaboration partners by role (within / within & outside / outside team)
page7_img_table_1.png.description: A heat-table of percentages showing where software engineers report collaborating with different roles: three columns list the fraction of respondents who interact with each role only within their team, with the role both within and outside their team, or only outside their team. Developers most often collaborate with other software engineers across team boundaries (e.g., “Software Engineer” = 41.3% within, 55.2% both, 3.6% outside; Senior Software Engineer = 33.0% / 63.0% / 3.9%), while engineering managers are the most within-team focused (Engineering Manager = 53.2% within, 40.9% both, 6.0% outside). By contrast, cross-functional specialists tend to be external collaborators (Scientist = 23.6% / 14.6% / 61.8%; Designer = 38.5% / 18.0% / 43.4%), and Operations Specialists are frequently engaged both inside and outside teams (16.0% / 63.7% / 20.3%).

page4_img_1.png.title: Heat map of seven clusters: developers' time across knowledge-worker actions
page4_img_1.png.description: A heat map showing how 868 surveyed software engineers cluster into seven groups (rows labeled Cluster 1–7 with cluster sizes) by the fraction of work time they spend in each adapted knowledge-worker action (11 columns). Each cell reports the average relative time (%) (top) and the average absolute hours/week (bottom) that cluster members spend on that action; the bottom row shows the population (ALL) averages (e.g., 21.4% / 9.1 hrs in the second action, 15.9% / 7.5 hrs in the fourth). The visualization makes the clusters’ distinguishing behaviors explicit: Cluster 2 (50 people) devotes ~39.0% (12.8 hrs) of its time to learning activities, Cluster 3 (125) concentrates ~46.1% (18.1 hrs) on analysis/debugging work, Cluster 1 (118) focuses ~38.4% (18.2 hrs) on authoring (writing), Cluster 5 (175) and Cluster 7 (93) show large shares on collaborative coding (≈30.2% / 14.6 hrs and 53.4% / 24.3 hrs respectively), and Cluster 6 (66) shows a notable peak (~27.6% / 8.9 hrs) in feedback/code-review style activities. These cluster-specific peaks illustrate the basis for the seven personas described in the paper (e.g., Continuous Learner, Investigator, Team Coder, Advisor).
